title: Degree and support bounds for Ext into a normalized algebraic dualizing complex
statement: Let $(A,\mathfrak m)$ be a nonzero commutative Noetherian local ring, and let $\omega\in D(A)$ be a normalized algebraic dualizing complex [def-per-algebraic-normalized-dualizing]. Let $M$ be a finitely generated $A$-module [def-weil-finitely-generated-module]. Put $E^i=H^i(R\operatorname{Hom}_A(M[0],\omega))$ for each $i\in\mathbf Z$ [def-pur-derived-internal-hom]. For an $A$-module $N$, define $\operatorname{Supp}_A(N)=\{\mathfrak q\subset A:\mathfrak q\text{ prime and }N_{\mathfrak q}\ne0\}$ [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime], and define its dimension as the supremum of the lengths of strict chains of prime ideals all in this support, with the empty support having dimension $-\infty$ [def-weil-pbc-krull-dimension-ring]. If $M=0$, every $E^i=0$. If $M\ne0$ and $d=\dim\operatorname{Supp}_A(M)\ge0$ is finite, then (1) $E^i=0$ for $i<-d$ or $i>0$, and (2) $\dim\operatorname{Supp}_A(E^i)\le -i$ for every integer $i$.

source.place: Tag 0A7U (lemma-sitting-in-degrees), parts (1) and (2); the zero-module case is stated explicitly.

proof.text: For every finite $A$-module $T$, write $D^i(T)=H^iR\operatorname{Hom}_A(T[0],\omega)$. Each $D^i(T)$ is finite: apply coherent derived-Hom preservation with $K=T[0]$ and $L=\omega$. The first has finite cohomology, while the defining conditions on the dualizing complex give finite cohomology and a bounded injective representative for the second. This checks the finiteness hypothesis needed in every later application of Nakayama.

Fix a bounded injective representative $J$ of $\omega$. It is K-injective by the bounded-below injective-complex lemma, so $R\operatorname{Hom}_A(T[0],\omega)$ is represented by $\operatorname{Hom}_A(T,J^\bullet)$. For a short exact sequence $0\to U\to V\to W\to0$, injectivity of each $J^n$ makes $0\to\operatorname{Hom}_A(W,J^\bullet)\to\operatorname{Hom}_A(V,J^\bullet)\to\operatorname{Hom}_A(U,J^\bullet)\to0$ degreewise exact: restriction is surjective by injectivity, and a map vanishing on $U$ factors uniquely through $W$. The cochain long-exact-sequence lemma therefore gives $\cdots\to D^i(W)\to D^i(V)\to D^i(U)\to D^{i+1}(W)\to\cdots$. If $U\to V$ is multiplication by $f$ on a module $T$, the map $D^i(T)\to D^i(T)$ is multiplication by $f$, since $\varphi(ft)=f\varphi(t)$ in every Hom term. Also $D^i(0)=0$, because its Hom complex is zero.

source.place: Tag 0A7U (lemma-sitting-in-degrees), parts (1) and (2); the zero-module case is stated explicitly.

proof.text:
First handle any finite-length module $T$. Its simple filtration has successive factors isomorphic to $\kappa=A/\mathfrak m$: for a nonzero vector $v$ in a simple module, $Av$ is the whole module and its annihilator is maximal, hence equals $\mathfrak m$ in this local ring. Normalization gives $D^i(\kappa)=0$ for $i
e0$ and $D^0(\kappa)\cong\kappa$. Induct along the finite simple filtration, starting with zero. Step 2 makes all nonzero-degree groups vanish at each extension, and in degree zero gives a short exact sequence whose two ends are the degree-zero groups of the factors. Thus $D^i(T)=0$ for $i
e0$; moreover $D^0(T)$ has a finite filtration with factors $\kappa$. For a prime $\mathfrak q
e\mathfrak m$, choose $a\in\mathfrak m\setminus\mathfrak q$: its invertibility at $\mathfrak q$ and its zero action on $\kappa$ give $\kappa_{\mathfrak q}=0$. Exactness of localization applied to the filtration shows $D^0(T)_{\mathfrak q}=0$. Consequently its support has dimension at most zero.

source.place: Tag 0A7Q (lemma-dualizing-finite-length), first sentence of proof: induction on length; only concentration and support are needed.

proof.text: We prove the two bounds simultaneously by strong induction on the finite integer $d=\dim\operatorname{Supp}(M)$ for nonzero finite modules. The zero-module assertion was proved in Step 2. For $d=0$, the finite-module support criterion makes $\operatorname{Supp}(M)=V(\operatorname{Ann}(M))$ stable under specialization. Every nonzero finite module has $\mathfrak m$ in its support: a proper annihilator is contained in the unique maximal ideal. If any different prime $\mathfrak q$ were in the support, $\mathfrak q\subsetneq\mathfrak m$ would be a chain of length one in it. Hence the support is $\{\mathfrak m\}$. The finite-length criterion applies, and Step 3 gives both assertions. Now fix $d>0$ and assume both assertions for every nonzero finite module of support dimension less than $d$.

source.place: Tag 0A7U (lemma-sitting-in-degrees), parts (1) and (2); the zero-module case is stated explicitly.

proof.text: First consider any nonzero finite module $T$ of support dimension $d$ which admits a nonzerodivisor $f\in\mathfrak m$. Set $Q=T/fT$. It is finite as a quotient, and nonzero by Nakayama, since $(f)\subseteq\mathfrak m$ is in the Jacobson radical. The support-dimension equality for a nonzerodivisor gives $\dim\operatorname{Supp}(Q)=d-1$, so the induction hypothesis applies to $Q$. The short exact sequence $0\to T\xrightarrow{f}T\to Q\to0$ gives, by Step 2, $\cdots\to D^i(Q)\to D^i(T)\xrightarrow{f}D^i(T)\to D^{i+1}(Q)\to\cdots$. Hence $D^i(T)/fD^i(T)$ injects into $D^{i+1}(Q)$. For $i<-d$ or $i\ge0$, $D^{i+1}(Q)=0$: its degree is respectively less than $-(d-1)$ or greater than zero. Nakayama, using Step 1, gives $D^i(T)=0$ in these degrees. This is slightly stronger than assertion (1) for such $T$.

source.place: Tag 0A7U (lemma-sitting-in-degrees), parts (1) and (2); the zero-module case is stated explicitly.

proof.text: For the support bound in this regular-element case, only $-d\le i\le-1$ remains. Put $P=D^i(T)$, a finite module by Step 1. Exactness of localization applied to the injection in Step 5 shows $\operatorname{Supp}(P/fP)\subseteq\operatorname{Supp}(D^{i+1}(Q))$. If $P=0$ there is nothing to prove. Otherwise Nakayama gives $P/fP\ne0$, and the one-equation support bound and the induction hypothesis give $\dim\operatorname{Supp}(P)\le\dim\operatorname{Supp}(P/fP)+1\le-(i+1)+1=-i$. The middle inequality follows directly from inclusion of supports and the chain definition of dimension. Together with Step 5 this proves both bounds for every module of dimension $d$ admitting such an $f$.

source.place: Tag 0A7U (lemma-sitting-in-degrees), parts (1) and (2); the zero-module case is stated explicitly.

proof.text:
For the original $M$, let $N=\{x\in M:\mathfrak m^n x=0	ext{ for some }n\ge1\}$ and $M'=M/N$. The set $N$ is a submodule: powers of an ideal form a decreasing sequence, so one common larger power kills any finite sum and all scalar multiples. It is finite by the Noetherian submodule lemma. Choosing finitely many generators of $N$ and a maximum of their annihilating exponents gives $\mathfrak m^rN=0$ for some $r\ge1$. Thus for $\mathfrak q
e\mathfrak m$, an element of $\mathfrak m\setminus\mathfrak q$ has a power annihilating $N$ and is invertible at $\mathfrak q$, so $N_{\mathfrak q}=0$. If $N
e0$, its support is contained in $\{\mathfrak m\}$ and the finite-length criterion applies. Step 3 (also valid for $N=0$) therefore shows that $D^i(N)=0$ for $i
e0$ and $\operatorname{Supp}(D^0(N))\subseteq\{\mathfrak m\}$.

source.place: Tag 0A7U (lemma-sitting-in-degrees), parts (1) and (2); the zero-module case is stated explicitly.

proof.text: Localization of $0\to N\to M\to M'\to0$ is exact, and Step 7 gives $M_{\mathfrak q}\cong M'_{\mathfrak q}$ for $\mathfrak q\ne\mathfrak m$. Since $d>0$, the support of $M$ is not contained in $\{\mathfrak m\}$; hence $M'\ne0$. The quotient $M'$ is finite, and its annihilator is proper, so the finite-module support criterion puts $\mathfrak m$ in its support as well. Thus $\operatorname{Supp}(M')=\operatorname{Supp}(M)$ and its dimension is $d$. The ideal $\mathfrak m$ is finitely generated by Noetherianity. The quotient-by-power-torsion lemma gives $M'[\mathfrak m]=0$, so no nonzero vector of $M'$ has annihilator $\mathfrak m$. Apply the nonzerodivisor-existence lemma to $M'$ to obtain $f\in\mathfrak m$ injective on $M'$. Steps 5 and 6 therefore prove both bounds for $M'$.

source.place: Tag 0A7U (lemma-sitting-in-degrees), parts (1) and (2); the zero-module case is stated explicitly.

proof.text: The sequence of Step 2 for $0\to N\to M\to M'\to0$ contains $D^i(M')\to D^i(M)\to D^i(N)$. If $i<-d$ or $i>0$, both outside groups vanish by Steps 7 and 8; thus $D^i(M)=0$, proving (1). Exactness after localization gives $\operatorname{Supp}(D^i(M))\subseteq\operatorname{Supp}(D^i(M'))\cup\operatorname{Supp}(D^i(N))$. For $i\ne0$ the second support is empty, so the dimension bound for $M'$ proves (2). For $i=0$, the first support has dimension at most zero and is closed by finiteness (Step 1) and the support criterion; in a local spectrum such a closed set is contained in $\{\mathfrak m\}$, by the chain argument of Step 4. The second support is also contained there by Step 7. Hence $\dim\operatorname{Supp}(D^0(M))\le0$. This completes the induction and both clauses, with empty supports assigned dimension $-\infty$ throughout.

The item keeps clauses (1) and (2) word for word, plus the M=0 case; it leaves out (3), the depth clause, which the citer does not use. The statement, stmt_deps and source are the same as the live unsplit node. All nine steps hold. Step 1: coherent-RHom finiteness applies to K=T[0] and L=omega, using the bounded-injective and finite-cohomology clauses of the definition. Step 2: J is K-injective, so RHom is Hom(T,J), with a degreewise exact sequence and a long exact sequence. Step 3: the finite-length case follows from normalization and the simple filtration, without Matlis duality. Step 4: the d=0 base uses Supp=V(Ann) and the 00L5 criterion. Step 5: a nonzerodivisor f gives dim Supp(T/fT)=d-1 (0B52 equality, option 2); Nakayama and the degree check give D^i=0 for i<-d and for i>=0 (D^0=0 is correct when depth>0). Step 6: the 0B52 bound needs no nonzerodivisor on Ext. Steps 7-9: M[m^inf] is killed by m^r and supported at m; 05EB and 00LL give f on M'; the Ext sequence finishes both clauses. Small cases check out: k[[t]] with omega=A[1] and M=A, k, A+k; a field; M=0. No duplicate (only the item and its citer carry 0A7U), no cycle, no SGA.
